_doc: The execution-profile document, whole. Copy it to
manager/local/profiles.json and edit, or point BOARD_AGENT_PROFILES at
a copy elsewhere. This file is documentation: core never reads it, and
a board with no document at all resolves on BOARD_AGENT_COMMANDS plus
the adapter's built-in git/gh grants — exactly the behaviour bench had
before profiles existed. Writing a document is how you get more; it is
never required.
It is machine-local on purpose. It names roots on THIS disk and
capabilities THIS adapter declares, so it belongs with the tool
(manager/local/ is gitignored) and not in the application's history.
Nothing here is ever committed, pushed or carried into a PR body.
WHAT A PROFILE IS RESOLVED FOR
One per launch intent: `work`, `act-pr`, `review`. An intent the
document says nothing about falls back to the legacy settings, so a
document may configure one intent and leave the others alone.
A PROFILE NARROWS; IT NEVER WIDENS
publication.commit/push/publish may be turned OFF for an intent that
has them and never ON for one that does not — `review` asking for
push is refused by name. The built-in git/gh grants per intent are
the adapter's own knowledge and are not a profile's to change.
WHAT 'commands' IS NOT
It is agent capability, and nothing else. A `manager/local/commands/`
executable is UI registration — a $ chip a person clicks — and being
registered there grants a headless run nothing: resolved profiles
list those separately, every one marked agentCapability: false.
And a `checks` entry is neither: it is a command BENCH runs on a
run's request, so the run is granted the shim that asks for it and
not the command itself.
COMMANDS, AND CHECKS
A `commands` grant is a PREFIX a model composes a command line
against. A `checks` entry is a NAME: the run asks for `unit`, bench
builds the argument list from this document and runs it with no
shell, and the evidence recorded is the exit status of bench's own
child process. Declaring a check is how a project stops taking an
agent's word for 'the tests passed'. Declare both, one, or neither.
HOW STRONGLY ANYTHING IS ENFORCED
A command grant becomes a prefix allow-rule in the adapter's rule
language. That narrows which command lines a run may launch. It is
NOT a sandbox — nothing confines a process already running — and the
resolved profile's `guarantees` block is the single place that says
so. `requires` is how you refuse to run without a real guarantee:
every word in it must be a capability the installed backend declares,
and a profile requiring one nothing enforces is refused rather than
run under a restriction that exists only in the prompt.
THE SETTINGS PRECEDENCE, IN ORDER
BOARD_AGENT_PROFILES > manager/local/profiles.json > the legacy
BOARD_AGENT_COMMANDS and the adapter's built-in grants. A document
that does not parse, or declares a `v` this bench does not read, is a
blocker on every intent — it does not quietly become the old policy.
CHECKING IT WITHOUT PAYING FOR A LAUNCH
Every refusal below is produced in milliseconds, so ask for it before
you pay for a run that would have told you:
python3 .task-manager/manager/board.py --doctor
python3 .task-manager/manager/board.py --doctor --help
or the ⚕ readiness chip in the board's header. It resolves every
intent through the resolver a launch rides, names the diagnostic code
and remedy for anything that would stop one, and — when you ask for
the active stages by name — runs the adapter's own generation and
bench's own check runner at a fixture it removes. It fixes nothing.
See 'Readiness: asking before paying' in AGENTS.md.
_doc_shared: intent that does not name its own. Handy for one brief every run must
read, or one check every intent may ask for.
_doc_checks: THE CHECKS BENCH RUNS ITSELF.
Declared once here, at the top level, and selected per intent by name
in that intent's `verify` list — so a check reviewed once is the same
check whichever intent asks for it. An intent with no `verify` has no
checks and is granted no shim.
name     what a run asks for, and what its evidence is filed under
run      one executable and fixed arguments. Quoting IS allowed
here, unlike in a `commands` grant: a grant becomes a
prefix allow-rule and a rule cannot see through a quote,
but bench splits a check itself and hands the result to
execve — so a path with spaces is expressible. What is
still refused is anything that makes one command line into
root     worktree (the card's own checkout), source (a detached
checkout of one exact commit that bench makes for the
verification and removes afterwards) or review (the
checkout bench pinned for a PR review — detached at the
head that pull request proposes, owned by that run for its
whole life). NOT `app`: a check never runs in the live
application. A `review`-rooted check is offered only to a
run that holds such a checkout, so `◔ review PR` may ask
for it and `◔ still true?` — which pins nothing and
reviews no pull request — simply is not offered it.
scopes   {name: [arguments]}. A run selects a scope BY NAME; the
arguments are yours and never the run's, which is what
keeps a model out of the argv.
prepare  names from the top-level `prepare` list, run before this
check in the same root. A required one failing is
`prepare-failed`, which is not a test failure.
timeout  seconds, narrowing BOARD_VERIFY_TIMEOUT and never widening
it. A timeout is recorded as `error`, never as a failure.
required whether a later gate should insist on it (declared; the
gate itself is a later member — `verified-outputs` is
still pending and a profile requiring it refuses).
REFUSED WHERE THIS FILE IS READ, before any process: a root of `app`,
a git subcommand that reshapes the repository (push, reset, worktree,
checkout, branch, config, clean, commit, …) because the execution
root shares its git metadata with every other worktree, an argument
whose basename reads as a credential, a scope that is not a name, and
a `verify` entry naming neither a check nor one of that intent's own
command grants.
THE COMPATIBILITY PATH: a `verify` entry naming one of the intent's
own `commands` grants resolves to a check built from that grant, so a
document written before bench could run anything keeps working.

_doc: A check a read-only review may ask for. It runs in a detached
checkout of the card's own commit that bench makes and removes,
because a review has no worktree and must never run a suite in
the live application.
checks.name: whitespace

_doc: A check against the code a pull request actually proposes. It
runs in the checkout bench pinned for the review — detached at
the reviewed head, which is the revision the verdict is about —
so its evidence goes stale the moment that head moves, and a
merged pull request makes it historical rather than current.
Only `◔ review PR` is offered it. A relevance check has no such
checkout and is not offered it, which is a note rather than a
blocker: declaring one must not take `◔ still true?` down.
checks.name: review-tests
checks.help: the project's own suite, against the proposed revision

_doc_prepare: Preparation steps, by name, run in the same isolated root as the
check that names them (or before every check of an intent that names
them in its own `prepare`). Same validation as a check.
required  true (default) means a failure stops the check and is
recorded as `prepare-failed` — a dependency that would
not install is not a test that failed. false means the
failure is noted and the check runs anyway.
network   declares that this step needs the network. Bench enforces
NO network boundary (`network-policy` is pending), so the
step gets whatever network this machine has and the
resolved profile says so out loud. A profile that wants
Where its writes go: bench points HOME, TMPDIR, XDG_*, PIP_CACHE_DIR,
NPM_CONFIG_CACHE, CARGO_HOME and the rest into a directory made for
this card's verifications, so a venv, node_modules or a build cache
lands there and not in anybody's home directory. That is where writes
are DIRECTED, not a boundary they are held inside.

prepare.name: deps
prepare.help: the project's own dependencies, into bench's isolated HOME

_doc: An approved readable input. `path` is <root>:<relative path>, with
the root one of worktree, app, work, tool — a word rather than a
path, because the document is read on a machine whose paths are
its own. Resolved, hashed and copied into a read-only bundle
before the model is invoked, so a later edit changes the NEXT run
and not this one.
Refused, fail-closed, every time: a path that is absolute or uses
'..', one that resolves outside its root through a link, a
directory (a directory grant is not a read-only guarantee), a
basename that reads as a credential, and anything over the
512 KiB cap. A required input that is missing or unreadable
refuses the launch by name, with a remedy. `"required": false`
turns that refusal into a note and changes nothing else.
Approval covers these files and nothing beside them. It is not
permission to edit them, to read what sits next to them, or to
publish their contents.
context.name: workflow-brief

_doc: A named command grant. `name` is its identity in the manifest,
the prompt and the UI. `run` is one executable and fixed
arguments — refused if it holds any of ; & | ` $ > < ( ) { }
* ? ! ~ # ' " \ [ ], because a prefix rule cannot see what a
shell would expand those into. The executable must be a bare
name resolved on PATH or an absolute path. `root` is which
approved root it runs in (default worktree).
commands.name: unit-tests

_doc_verify: Which of the document's checks this intent may ask bench to run.
Names only — the definitions are at the top level. Declaring one
adds bench's own `bench-verify` shim to this intent's grants and
nothing else: the run may ask, and may not run the command.
A name here that is neither a declared check nor one of this
intent's own command grants REFUSES the launch, by name. A
requirement that resolves to nothing is indistinguishable from a
check that will never run, and that is the reading this exists to
_doc_prepare_intent: Preparation this intent needs before ANY of its checks, as
against a check's own `prepare` which runs only before it. Names

_doc: The intent the legacy arrangement had no answer for: it got a
hardcoded grant set inside each adapter and nothing else. Here it
is a profile like the others — it is granted no project commands
unless this names them, and the only thing it publishes is its
verdict.
WHERE it runs depends on which review it is, and bench decides
rather than this file. `◔ review PR` is pinned a detached
checkout of the exact head its pull request proposes and runs
there; `◔ still true?` reviews no pull request, pins nothing and
runs in the application checkout as it always did. The resolved
profile says which, in `cwd.policy` — `review` or `app`.
It may still VERIFY. A `verify` list gives a read-only run the
shim and nothing else: it can ask bench to run a `source`- or
`review`-rooted check and gains no commit and no push rule
anywhere in the generated permission document. Verifying is not
committing, and this is where the two stop being one question.
